idiom_name: trait default methods using Self + monomorphized generic bounds (static dispatch by default)
implementation_notes: Rust does not need CRTP: a trait's methods can mention Self, so a 'base that refers to the implementing type' is simply a trait with default methods, and generic code constrained by that trait is monomorphized - the Rust Book calls the result static dispatch, with no vtable indirection and full inlining. dyn Trait is the explicit opt-in to dynamic dispatch (fat pointer plus vtable), and the object-safety rules (methods mentioning Self beyond the receiver, associated constants, generic methods) mark exactly where a trait can no longer be used behind a pointer. Express 'the implementing type' as Self and put per-implementation data in the impl; reserve CRTP-style trickery for porting C++ idioms.
pitfalls: A trait whose methods mention Self outside the receiver is not object-safe, so the same trait cannot always be used both statically (T: Trait) and dynamically (dyn Trait); split it or keep Self outside the object-safe core.
Monomorphization duplicates code per concrete type: heavy generic bounds grow binary size and compile time, and switching to dyn is the usual remedy when that dominates.
An inherent method with the same name as a trait default method silently wins over the trait version, so behaviour can change without any override warning.
